I am 74 years old. I have farmed my land in Quzhou County since I was a young man. My father taught me, and I have seen every kind of weather this plain can throw at us. I did not finish high school, but I do not need a diploma to read the soil and the sky. At my age, I do not chase new tricks. I stick to what feeds my family.

It is early spring. My winter wheat went into the ground last October, right after the autumn rains. Every year in Quzhou, we do the same rotation: winter wheat followed by summer maize. That is the system that works on this land. I have about five mu — enough to manage without killing myself, and some of the bigger plots I let my son farm now. 

For the wheat, I will apply the spring topdressing when the wheat turns green, probably urea mixed with a little compound fertilizer. I will irrigate three times: once at green-up, once at jointing, and once at grain filling if the spring turns dry. The wheat stubble will stay on the field after harvest — no point burning it anymore. For the maize, I will plant a hybrid variety, likely something like Nongda 372, right after the wheat comes off in early June. I will spread compound fertilizer as basal dressing before planting, then sidedress with urea when the maize is knee-high. I will irrigate twice for the maize: once right after sowing to ensure germination, and once at the big喇叭口 stage. I will spray pesticides twice on each crop — once for weeds and once for insects — but I do not spray blindly. I walk the fields and look. Tillage? I rotary-tilled the wheat field last autumn. For the maize, I will plant directly into the wheat stubble. No-tillage saves time, fuel, and my back.

I use improved seeds for wheat and hybrid seeds for maize. The yields have been good these past years with the irrigation from our wells. I expect around 950 jin per mu for wheat and about 1,000 jin per mu for maize if the weather holds.
